The Authentic Name

Why ēl.com is the correct form

Canaanite Original

Ἠλ

The name in its original Canaanite form. A name that carries the full phonetic weight of its source tradition.

ASCII Constraint

EL

Stripped of its identity, the name was reduced to plain Latin letters. The original orthography — stress, length, breathing — was erased by systems that only understand A-Z.

Unicode Restoration

Ēl

The Unicode restoration recovers what ASCII destroyed. This is philological accuracy — not decoration. The domain encodes to Punycode, but the browser displays the truth.

Valid Scholarly Variations
El ēl

Each variant is an attested scholarly orthography. The owned form is the active domain; others are historically valid alternatives.

Punycode Encoding
ēl.com → xn--l-oia.com

The non-ASCII characters in Ēl are encoded while the ASCII remains visible. To the DNS, it is Punycode. To humanity, it is Ēl.

Tier Classification

Why Ēl is classified as Tier-2 Macron-Preserving

The Canaanite original Ἠλ contains only length (macron vowel). This makes it a single-tier Tier-2 name. The Unicode restoration preserves what can be preserved — honoring the single feature that distinguishes it from plain ASCII.

04a

Unicode Registration Note

Why this flagship preserves length with a macron

The Canaanite name Ēl contains a long vowel /ē/, corresponding to Hebrew אֵל and Common Semitic *ʾil-. The macron is the standard scholarly way to mark this length in transliteration.

No pharyngeal consonant occurs in this name, so the Egyptian Ain workaround used for Baꜥal, ꜥAnat, and ꜥAsherah is not needed here. The registrable form simply preserves the long vowel that distinguishes Ēl from plain El.

06

Mythology & Lore

The Canaanite father of gods

In the Ugaritic texts, El (Ilu) sits at the head of the divine assembly. He is Bull El (tr il), a title of strength and fertility, and he dwells “at the source of the rivers, in the midst of the meeting-place of the deeps.”

El is the husband of Asherah and the father of Baꜥal, ꜥAnat, Mot, Yam, and the other gods. He is not a stormy warrior like his son Baꜥal; he is the wise, gray-bearded patriarch whose word establishes kingship. In the Baal Cycle, it is El who finally ratifies Baꜥal’s authority after Baꜥal defeats Yam, the sea.

His epithets reveal a compassionate figure: El the Kind, El the Compassionate, and Father of Years (ab šnm). He represents the abstract, transcendent high god — the divine as such — rather than a local mountain or storm.

07

Pronunciation

How to say the name

Reconstructed: /ˈeːl/ (long close-mid front vowel, followed by /l/).

The macron over the e marks a long vowel, matching the Canaanite / Semitic ʾēl. In modern English contexts it is often pronounced like the letter “L,” but the ancient form had a distinct, sustained /ē/ sound.

09

Syncretism

El across cultures

Hebrew Bible: El becomes the generic word for God and appears in epithets such as El Elyon (God Most High), El Shaddai (God Almighty), and Elohim. The name Israel means “he who strives with El.”

Greek interpretatio: Philo of Byblos, quoted by Eusebius, equates the Phoenician high god El with the Greek Titan Krónos — both are the wise, aged father of the gods.

Arabic: The common Semitic root survives in ʾilāh (“god”) and, with the definite article, Allāh — a distant but real linguistic cousin.

Roman world: In some western Phoenician contexts El was syncretized with Saturn, the old god of sowing and time.

10

Cultural Legacy

Where the name lives today

El survives in countless names — Gabriel, Michael, Daniel, Ezekiel, Israel, Samuel, Joel — and in the very word “God” as used in biblical tradition.

The Canaanite idea of a single high god named El also provided a theological vocabulary that later monotheisms adapted. When the biblical text speaks of El, it is often borrowing the title of the deity who once sat above Baꜥal and Asherah on Mount Saphon.
